system: You are given a list of CRITIQUES someone expected a reviewer to raise about a document, and the FINDINGS actual reviewers raised. For each expected critique, decide whether any finding raises it in substance. Reply with JSON only: {"raised": {"1": true|false, ...}}
message:
CRITIQUES:
1. The 15% app price premium is an assumption.** The brief doesn't give it, and the "markup dropped" scenario depends heavily on it
2. The brief contradicts itself, and the memo picks one reading.** It says direct orders "tend to be larger" but also that prices would drop on the direct channel. A reviewer may argue direct baskets could be bigger in item count
3. The 20% volume loss after the cap is a guess.** No data shows how customers will respond to the new app fees
4. Lost orders aren't all lost.** Some lost delivery customers would switch to pickup or dine-in, so the cost of exiting is overstated
5. The 65% cost is treated as fully variable.** Part of kitchen labor is fixed, so the contribution figures are understated in both scenarios
6. Several costs are left out:** card processing, courier tips, refunds and failed deliveries, and whether a white-label courier can cover late-night hours near campus
7. It is a year-one view only.** The $60,000 in marketing is one-time, and retention may improve over time, so a multi-year comparison would narrow the gap. It likely wouldn't close it against the post-cap figures
8. Everything uses 2025 volumes.** There is no growth or seasonality, and no figures for individual locations, even though the memo's 2028 decision point is set by location
9. Cutting marketing to $20,000 is untested.** It may produce lower direct adoption than the scenarios assume
10. The ordinance details are assumed.** The memo assumes all six locations fall inside the city's jurisdiction and that the 15% cap covers all fees, not just the base commission
11. The "late-night" warning is unverified.** It rests on the general manager's claim, not on order-time data
12. The owners' framing goes unchallenged.** Commissions are about 5% of sales, so food and labor are larger costs. Calling commissions "our single biggest controllable cost" may be overstated

FINDINGS:
- The full-exit scenario assumes Fennel absorbs the entire $8.50 courier cost, while the recommendation (Action 1) charges customers a delivery fee, so the two scenarios use inconsistent fee assumptions.
- Applying the same delivery fee to the exit scenario raises direct margin to about $10–12 per order and narrows the advantage of post-cap apps from roughly $270K–$390K to roughly $60K–$230K, undermining the 'Why a full exit doesn't pay' section as written.
- The memo does not explicitly argue that a delivery fee would push retention below the 40–60% range, which is the counterargument needed to justify the different fee assumptions.
- The headline '$90,000–$120,000 worse off' range is selectively narrow because it omits the memo's own worse cases (markup dropped at 50% retention, or 40% retention), which put losses near $146K–$169K.
- The recommended hybrid option is never costed: the memo does not show what a shifted order earns direct with the fee versus on an app post-cap ($7.60).
- The memo does not note that the $18K software cost needs some direct volume to pay back.
- The $460K post-cap figure is annualized even though 2027 gets only 10 months of the cap.
- The memo does not consider whether app menu prices should come down once commissions fall to 15%.
- The 15% app price premium is an unflagged assumption.
- The 20% app volume-loss assumption is defended without stating the break-even point (apps win unless volume falls by more than about 60%).
- Omitted costs matter: card processing (~3%, about $1.14 per order, roughly a quarter of the direct margin) falls only on the direct side, and late-night courier coverage near campus is an operational risk.
- The analysis covers only year one; year two without marketing ($145K–$174K) is not reported.
- The $20K marketing spend is untested and should be framed as a deliberate low-cost test rather than a full migration push.
- The memo does not caveat that lost orders may shift to pickup or dine-in, or that fixed labor makes lost orders cost less than modeled.
- The memo relies on 2025 volumes and gives no per-location figures, even though Action 5's decision rule is set by location.
- The memo does not address jurisdiction or fee scope; if the cap covers only base commission and apps shift costs into other fees, the $460K is overstated.
- The late-night demand claim is unverified and could be checked cheaply with app order-time data.
- The exit scenario assumes customers pay nothing toward the $8.50 courier cost while the recommended option charges a delivery fee, so the '$90K–$120K worse off' headline rests on an inconsistent assumption.
- The recommended option is never costed, including no breakeven estimate of how many orders must shift to the direct channel to cover roughly $38K in year-one costs.
- The retention range is selectively presented, omitting the consultants' 40% lower bound, under which year one would be about $146K worse than today.
- Card processing fees (about 3%, roughly $1.10 per order) are mentioned but not subtracted from the direct per-order margin.
- The 15% app price premium is the memo's own assumption presented as fact, and the 'markup dropped' result depends on whether food cost is treated as fixed in dollars or as 65% of a lower price.
- The memo interprets 'direct orders tend to be larger' as reflecting lower prices without acknowledging it could mean more items per order.
- Post-cap figures are full-year numbers presented as 2027 results even though the cap starts March 1, so the blended 2027 figure should be about $414K rather than $460K.
- The claim that 68% of customers had never ordered before drops the brief's qualifier 'before that year.'
- The claim that apps are the 'largest source of new customers' is not supported by the brief.
- The late-night business concern rests on one GM's warning rather than order-time data and is not attributed.
- The 20% volume loss from app customer fees is an illustrative assumption not labeled as such.
- The memo assumes without saying so that the cap covers all six locations and all app charges, including marketing and service fees.
- The exit cost is overstated because some lost app customers would switch to pickup or dine-in rather than disappearing.
- Treating the 65% cost as fully variable ignores fixed kitchen labor and understates contribution in every scenario.
- The analysis covers only year one, ignoring that the $60K marketing spend is one-time and that retention may grow over time.
- Everything uses 2025 aggregate volumes with no per-location figures, even though the January 2028 decision is to be made location by location.
- Cutting marketing to $20K is untested and may reduce direct-channel adoption.
- Pausing app ordering at peak hours (Action 3) gives up post-cap contribution, and the memo does not acknowledge this trade-off.
- A January 2028 review may come too late to influence the College Ave lease renewal decision.
- The memo does not test the owners' claim that commissions are the 'biggest controllable cost,' even though commissions are only about 5% of sales.
- Courier tips, refunds, failed deliveries, and whether a white-label courier can cover late-night hours near campus are not costed or addressed.
response: {"raised": {"1": true, "2": true, "3": true, "4": true, "5": true, "6": true, "7": true, "8": true, "9": true, "10": true, "11": true, "12": true}}
